verses: A Psalm of thanksgiving. Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth.
Serve the LORD with gladness; come into His presence with joyful songs.
Know that the LORD is God. It is He who made us, and we are His; we are His people, and the sheep of His pasture.
Enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise; give thanks to Him and bless His name.
For the LORD is good, and His loving devotion endures forever; His faithfulness continues to all generations.
title: Through the Gates
season_line: Two weeks before Thanksgiving, with the trees nearly bare and the holidays starting to fill the calendar, this ancient song invites us to practice thanks before the feast arrives.
big_idea: We belong to God before we do anything for Him, so gratitude is the gate we walk through, not a mood we wait for.
frame: Most days, thanks comes last. We get through the to-do list and, if things went well, we feel grateful. This psalm turns that around. It starts with who God is and whose we are, and lets gladness flow from there, even on a gray Thursday with a full inbox. Jesus later calls Himself the Good Shepherd who knows His sheep by name, so the people of this pasture include us. Carry that into the day: you are not earning your place with God. You already belong, so walk in thankful.

carry.text: Know that the LORD is God. It is He who made us, and we are His; we are His people, and the sheep of His pasture.

glance.head: A call to joy
glance.line: The whole earth is invited to shout, serve, and sing to the LORD with gladness.

glance.head: Know whose you are
glance.line: The LORD is God, He made us, and we belong to Him like sheep in His care.

glance.head: Enter with thanks
glance.line: Come into God's presence giving thanks, because He is good and His love and faithfulness never run out.

understand: Psalm 100 was likely sung as worshipers came up to the temple in Jerusalem, passing through its gates into the courtyards. The heading calls it a psalm of thanksgiving, possibly sung alongside a thank offering. It is short, but it covers all of worship: joy, service, knowing God, and gratitude.

Notice that the center of the psalm is a fact, not a feeling: we did not make ourselves, and we are His. The picture of sheep and pasture runs all through Scripture. God promised to shepherd His scattered people Himself ({{Ezekiel 34:11-16|Ezekiel 34:11–16}}), and Jesus said He is the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep and gathers others into the flock too ({{John 10:11-16|John 10:11–16}}).

The psalm opens to all the earth, not just Israel. That fits God's plan from the start to bless every nation through Abraham ({{Genesis 12:1-3|Genesis 12:1–3}}). The reason for all this joy is simple: God is good, His loving devotion lasts forever, and His faithfulness reaches every generation. Yesterday's reading reminded us our lives are short; today we see why that makes us glad rather than anxious.

word.gloss: Todah means giving thanks out loud, often as a public acknowledgment of what God has done. It was also the name of a thank offering, so it points to gratitude that is spoken and shown, not just felt.

glow: His faithfulness continues to all generations

god.short: Each time you walk through a door today, thank God for one specific thing.
god.full: Let every doorway today be a small gate. As you pass through, at home, work, or a store, quietly thank God for one specific gift, even a small one.
god.why: The psalm pictures entering God's gates with thanks; see {{Hebrews 13:15|Hebrews 13:15}} on offering praise continually.

together.short: Say to each other, out loud: 'We are His.'
together.full: Before you part this morning, look at each other and say the line from verse 3: we are His. Let it be the first thing true about your day.

others.short: Text someone who may be alone at Thanksgiving and ask about their plans.
others.full: Think of a neighbor, coworker, or friend who might spend Thanksgiving alone this year. Send a short text asking how they are spending the day, and leave the door open.
others.why: The psalm invites all the earth into God's courts; Jesus calls us to widen the table too ({{Luke 14:12-14|Luke 14:12–14}}).

tonight: Where do we tend to serve God out of duty more than gladness, and what might change if we started from the truth that we are His?

more.line: Jesus, the Good Shepherd who knows His sheep.
A sister psalm: come, worship, we are His flock.
Praise and doing good as everyday offerings.
